examinerBank.question: Walk me through your differential diagnosis for this acute hot swollen knee, and how you would rank them.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Septic arthritis is the leading and most dangerous diagnosis given acute onset, fever, systemic upset, immunosuppression from unsuppressed HIV, and a possible skin portal of entry — this must be actively excluded first. Gout is possible given acute severe monoarthropathy but is against by knee being less typical than the 1st MTP, no prior episodes, and normal urate. Reactive arthritis is considered given his HIV status but there is no preceding GI/GU infection or extra-articular features. TB arthritis is possible in this high-burden, immunosuppressed setting but usually has a more indolent course, against the 2-day acute onset here. RA is unlikely as this is monoarticular and acute rather than symmetrical and insidious.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Expects a ranked list with reasoning linking each differential explicitly to case features, not just a name-list. Septic arthritis must be named first and justified as needing urgent exclusion.

examinerBank.question: Why must you aspirate the joint before or immediately alongside starting antibiotics, rather than starting antibiotics first?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Antibiotics can rapidly sterilise the synovial fluid, dropping the yield of Gram stain and culture and making it far harder to confirm the causative organism and its sensitivities. Aspiration (and blood cultures) should be obtained as close to simultaneously with, but ideally just before, the first antibiotic dose so that the diagnosis and organism are not lost, unless the patient is critically septic and needs immediate empirical treatment.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Tests understanding of correct sequencing — analogous to the gout teaching point that treatment sequencing is an exam trap. Should mention blood cultures too.

examinerBank.question: Why is his HIV status and CD4 count so important in this presentation?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Immunosuppression from a low CD4 count (here 142) impairs opsonisation and neutrophil/macrophage function, increasing susceptibility to more severe, atypical and rapidly destructive septic arthritis, and broadens the differential to include TB and unusual organisms. It also affects management — need to address ART adherence, consider co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and have a lower threshold for aggressive source control.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants both the pathophysiological rationale for increased susceptibility and the downstream management implications (ART restart, OI prophylaxis).

examinerBank.question: Explain the pathophysiology behind why he is holding the knee in a fixed flexed position and refusing to let you move it.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: The purulent effusion distends the joint capsule; partial flexion is the position that maximises intracapsular volume and therefore minimises capsular tension and pain, so the patient adopts and guards this posture involuntarily. Direct inflammatory sensitisation of joint nociceptors from cytokines and bacterial products also lowers the pain threshold to any movement.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Pathophysiology-mechanism question — wants capsular volume/pressure relationship, not just 'it hurts'.

examinerBank.question: His synovial Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. How does this change your empirical antibiotic choice, and what would you do while awaiting final culture and sensitivities?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Gram-positive cocci in clusters suggests Staphylococcus aureus, the most common cause of septic arthritis; empirical therapy should cover this (e.g. IV cloxacillin/flucloxacillin, or vancomycin if MRSA risk is high locally). Continue empirical broad cover initially if there is any doubt, then narrow once final culture and sensitivities are available, and reassess clinical response (fever, CRP trend, joint findings) to judge duration and route of therapy.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants organism-directed reasoning and safety-netting language about narrowing therapy once sensitivities return.

framework: acute hot swollen joint: mono- vs oligo- vs polyarthritis, red-flag screen for septic arthritis before assuming crystal/inflammatory cause

patient.name: Bongani Mthembu
patient.personality: stoic but clearly in pain, tries to minimise how unwell he feels, reluctant to mention his HIV status unless asked directly
patient.openingLine: Doctor, my knee is so swollen and painful, I can't even bend it or put weight on it.

presentingComplaint: 2-day history of acute right knee pain, swelling and fever, unable to weight-bear

history.fact: Knee pain and swelling started suddenly 2 days ago and has rapidly worsened
Only the right knee is affected — no other joints painful or swollen
Pain is severe (9/10), worse with any movement, cannot bend or straighten the knee, cannot weight-bear
Felt hot and shivery yesterday, sweaty overnight, has not measured temperature
No injury, fall or knock to the knee before symptoms started
Noticed a small cut on his shin from a fence about a week before the knee started, which looked infected and oozed pus for a few days
No previous problems with this or any other joint, no gout, no arthritis before
Diagnosed HIV positive two years ago, on ART but admits he has missed clinic visits and hasn't collected his tablets in about 4 months
No intravenous drug use, no recent injections other than clinic ART depot
No urethral discharge, no genital symptoms, no recent new sexual partners
No cough, no night sweats beyond the fever illness, no known TB contact, has not lost weight recently
No diabetes, no hypertension, no other chronic illness besides HIV
Should be on TLD (tenofovir/lamivudine/dolutegravir) but has not collected in 4 months; takes no other regular medication, occasional paracetamol
Smokes occasionally (about 2 cigarettes a day), drinks alcohol on weekends, lives alone in a rented room in KwaMashu, works night shifts as a security guard
No family history of arthritis, gout or autoimmune disease
No rash, no eye redness, no diarrhoea or GI symptoms preceding this, no back pain

examination.general: Uncomfortable, guarding the right leg, lying still to avoid moving the knee. Mildly diaphoretic. No peripheral lymphadenopathy. Oral mucosa clear, no thrush.
examination.respiratory: Clear, equal air entry bilaterally, no added sounds
examination.cardio: Tachycardic, normal heart sounds, no murmurs, warm peripheries, brisk cap refill
examination.neuro: Alert and orientated, distal neurovascular status of the right leg intact (sensation and pulses preserved), no focal deficit

investigations.name: Knee joint aspiration — synovial fluid microscopy, Gram stain and culture
investigations.result: Turbid yellow fluid, WCC 65,000/µL with 92% neutrophils, Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters, culture pending

investigations.name: Synovial fluid crystal analysis
investigations.result: No urate or calcium pyrophosphate crystals seen

investigations.name: Blood cultures
investigations.result: Pending at time of assessment; drawn before antibiotics given

investigations.name: U&E/creatinine
investigations.result: Normal, eGFR >90 (baseline before any nephrotoxic antibiotic dosing)

investigations.name: Knee X-ray
investigations.result: Soft tissue swelling and joint effusion, no bony erosion or fracture, joint space preserved

for: possible portal of entry via recent skin wound
grade 4 tenderness, refusal to move joint

against: systemic sepsis picture more prominent than typical gout flare
fluid is purulent with organisms on Gram stain, not sterile inflammatory
no TB contact or constitutional symptoms
Gram stain already shows bacteria, fluid grossly purulent
no prior RA history, no small joint involvement

pathophys.acute hot swollen joint: Haematogenous or direct inoculation of bacteria (often Staph aureus) into the synovium triggers a rapid neutrophilic inflammatory response; synovial proliferation and purulent effusion raise intra-articular pressure and pH changes plus bacterial/host proteases rapidly degrade cartilage
pathophys.fever and systemic upset: Bacteraemia and local cytokine release (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha) from the infected joint act on the hypothalamus to raise the temperature set-point and drive a systemic inflammatory response
pathophys.severe pain with refusal to move the joi: Capsular distension from the purulent effusion plus direct inflammatory sensitisation of joint nociceptors causes pain at rest and on minimal motion, with reflex muscle guarding held in the position of maximum capsular volume (partial flexion) to minimise pressure
pathophys.fixed flexion posture: Partial flexion maximises intracapsular volume and minimises capsular tension, an involuntary pain-avoidance posture in any large joint effusion
pathophys.increased susceptibility in HIV/immunosu: Low CD4 count impairs opsonisation, neutrophil and macrophage function and adaptive immune surveillance, permitting more aggressive, atypical and rapidly destructive joint infection with a lower threshold for haematogenous seeding

staging: WHO HIV clinical stage 3 (unsuppressed viraemia on interrupted ART, CD4 142); acute bacterial (septic) monoarthritis of the right knee, native joint

immediate: Do not give antibiotics before aspiration unless patient is septic/unstable — aspirate joint first for microscopy, Gram stain and culture
Take blood cultures before starting antibiotics

Start empirical IV antibiotics per local protocol (e.g. IV cloxacillin/flucloxacillin, or IV ceftriaxone if Gram-negative/immunosuppressed risk considered) pending culture results, adjust once organism and sensitivities known
Urgent orthopaedic referral for consideration of surgical washout/arthrotomy or repeat aspiration
Immobilise/rest the joint, analgesia (avoid delaying source control for pain control)
Mark and monitor for compartment/systemic sepsis deterioration (repeat vitals, escalate if hypotensive)
definitive: Prolonged antibiotic course (typically IV 2 weeks then oral to complete 4-6 weeks total, guided by clinical response and CRP trend)
Surgical washout if poor response to aspiration/antibiotics alone, or if very purulent/loculated on aspiration
Re-engage HIV care: recommence ART (TLD), address adherence barriers, and coordinate CD4/viral load follow-up
Screen and treat for other opportunistic infections given CD4 142 (e.g. co-trimoxazole preventive therapy if not already on it)
supportive: Physiotherapy once infection controlled to restore range of motion and prevent joint stiffness/contracture
Adherence counselling and treatment supporter for ART
Wound care for the antecedent shin lesion
Pain control with regular analgesia (paracetamol ± short-course opioid if severe) plus rest/splintage acutely
followUp: Serial CRP and clinical joint review to gauge response to antibiotics
Repeat aspiration if not improving after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
Orthopaedic follow-up for joint function assessment
HIV clinic follow-up: viral load re-check at 3-6 months post ART resumption, CD4 monitoring, adherence support

stationChecklist.item: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, gains consent, explains examination
Establishes the joint pattern — confirms this is a single joint (monoarthritis) and asks about other joints
stationChecklist.answer: Right knee only, no other joints involved
stationChecklist.why: Mono- vs oligo- vs polyarthritis is the entry point to the whole framework

stationChecklist.item: Characterises onset/duration and screens for red flags of an acute hot joint (fever, systemic upset, immunosuppression)
stationChecklist.answer: Sudden 2-day onset, fever, rigors, known HIV with poor ART adherence
stationChecklist.why: Any acute hot swollen single joint must be treated as septic arthritis until excluded

stationChecklist.item: Asks about possible portal of entry/precipitant (trauma, skin breach, IVDU, recent infection)
stationChecklist.answer: Recent infected cut on the shin about a week before onset
stationChecklist.why: Identifies likely haematogenous or contiguous source of joint sepsis

stationChecklist.item: Asks HIV status, ART use and adherence directly and sensitively
stationChecklist.answer: HIV positive 2 years, on ART but defaulted for 4 months
stationChecklist.why: Immunosuppression changes pre-test probability, severity and organism spectrum of septic arthritis

stationChecklist.item: Screens for alternative causes: prior gout/arthritis history, morning stiffness pattern, other joint/systemic clues (rash, eye, GI/GU symptoms, TB contact)
stationChecklist.answer: No prior joint disease, no rash/eye symptoms, no TB contact or weight loss
stationChecklist.why: Differentiates from gout, reactive arthritis, RA and TB arthritis in the framework

stationChecklist.item: Performs systematic look-feel-move-measure-compare examination of the knee, including tenderness grading and assessment of effusion
stationChecklist.answer: Grossly swollen, erythematous, warm knee, ballottable effusion, grade 4 tenderness, fixed ~20 degree flexion, severely restricted ROM
stationChecklist.why: Systematic examination technique with formal tenderness grading is an explicitly taught exam skill

stationChecklist.item: Checks distal neurovascular status and looks for a source (skin breach, wound) near the joint
stationChecklist.answer: Neurovascularly intact distally; healing scar on shin from prior wound
stationChecklist.why: Excludes compartment/vascular compromise and confirms possible entry source

stationChecklist.item: Generates a ranked differential (septic arthritis first, then gout, reactive arthritis, TB arthritis, RA) with reasoning linking to findings
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning with red-flag exclusion is the core exam philosophy

stationChecklist.item: States that joint aspiration (with microscopy, Gram stain, culture) must be performed before or urgently alongside starting antibiotics, plus blood cultures first
stationChecklist.answer: Aspirate turbid fluid, WCC 65,000 with 92% neutrophils, Gram-positive cocci in clusters; blood cultures sent before antibiotics
stationChecklist.why: Sequencing trap — aspirate/cultures before antibiotics to avoid sterilising the diagnostic sample, mirrors the gout-sequencing teaching point in the framework

stationChecklist.item: Requests FBC, CRP/ESR, HIV test/CD4, U&E, and knee X-ray
stationChecklist.answer: WCC and CRP markedly raised, CD4 142, unsuppressed viral load, X-ray shows effusion only, no erosion
stationChecklist.why: Standard work-up for an acute hot joint and to stage HIV-related immunosuppression

stationChecklist.item: Outlines immediate management: source control (aspiration ± washout), empirical IV antibiotics after cultures taken, urgent orthopaedic referral, analgesia/immobilisation
stationChecklist.answer: IV antibiotics per protocol after aspirate/blood cultures, orthopaedic referral for washout, rest and analgesia
stationChecklist.why: Septic arthritis is an orthopaedic emergency requiring urgent source control plus antibiotics

stationChecklist.item: Addresses HIV re-engagement: restart ART, adherence counselling, co-trimoxazole consideration given CD4 <200
stationChecklist.answer: Recommence TLD, adherence support, screen for other OIs given CD4 142
stationChecklist.why: Underlying immunosuppression must be addressed as part of definitive and supportive management
